To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the use of image analysis to support research into Arabidopsis thalia is a challenging vision problem; (ii) there are a number of useful measurements that can be obtained from image analysis, but (iii) the most useful measurements are obtained by leaf-level segmentation; and (iv) the use of leaf-level segmentation makes it a problem that is well worth solving.
image analysis can make a significant contribution to plant biology research and that this contribution will be maximized if the computer vision and biology communities collaborate closely.

developing methods for computer vision that will allow the automated extraction of quantitative data from images of plant growth.
the use of computer vision techniques to support biological research.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a system for the segmentation of leaves in Arabidopsis thalia images that is robust to changes in leaf shape and lighting, and that is able to produce a segmentation that is accurate enough to allow the extraction of measurements that are useful to biologists.
we have developed an image segmentation system that is capable of segmenting leaves of the model plant Arabidopsis Thaliana.
we have developed a system for automated segmentation of leaves from images, and have used this to measure the area of individual leaves, the total leaf area and the total area of the plant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of computer vision techniques to study plants is a promising and important field of research.

the use of computer vision in biological research can be a two-way street: computer vision researchers can learn from the biological problems they tackle and the biologists can benefit from the computer vision techniques that are developed to tackle them.

there are many interesting problems to be solved in computer vision that can be tackled by working with the Arabidopsis community, and that there is a clear need for more computer vision researchers to become involved.
